_comment: Test fixture, derived from EXAMPLE_NOTEBOOK in backend/app/schemas/notebook.py and extended to exercise the renderer: three topic groups (so breakOnTopic produces >=3 pages), all three importance levels, a LaTeX formula, and a 24-item bullet_list that cannot fit on one page and must split with a '(contd.)' marker. This is the fixture that should LOOK like a real student's notebook — judge the handwriting illusion here. For type coverage (every schema type, awkward inputs, mid-element splits of the drawn types) see all-elements.json instead. The 'flowchart' and 'comparison' here were placeholders in v1 and are now really drawn.

elements.meaning: A search algorithm that finds a target by repeatedly halving the search space.
elements.example: Find 7 in [1,3,5,7,9] — check middle 5, go right, find 7.

elements.text: Only works on SORTED arrays. Always verify before applying.

elements.title: Advantages
items: Fast — eliminates half the array each step
O(log n) vs O(n) for linear search
Works well on large sorted datasets

elements.text: Computing mid as (low + high) / 2 overflows on large arrays in fixed-width integer languages. This bug shipped in java.util.Arrays for nine years.

elements.title: Every place an off-by-one hides
items: Initialising high to n instead of n-1
Using low < high when the loop needs low <= high
Forgetting to move past mid, so the range never shrinks
Returning low when the target is absent instead of -1
Assuming the array is non-empty before the first read
Comparing with == on floating-point values
Letting mid be computed before the emptiness check
Rounding mid down when the recurrence assumes rounding up
Mixing inclusive and exclusive bounds in the same function
Shrinking by mid rather than mid + 1 on the right branch
Shrinking by mid rather than mid - 1 on the left branch
Treating a signed length as unsigned
Searching a rotated array with the unrotated comparison
Using the wrong comparator for a descending sort
Assuming duplicates resolve to the first match
Assuming duplicates resolve to the last match
Trusting that the input was actually sorted
Recursing without a base case for the empty range
Blowing the stack on a recursive version for huge inputs
Reading arr[mid] after the bounds have already crossed
Caching the length across a mutation of the array
Applying it to a linked list and losing O(log n) entirely
Reusing a stale mid from the previous iteration
Writing the tests against the same wrong mental model

elements.meaning: A condition true before and after every loop iteration — here, that the target lies within [low, high] if it is present at all.

points: Pick one bound convention and never mix them
State the loop invariant before writing the loop

items: Unsorted data — sorting first costs O(n log n)
Very small arrays, where linear scan wins on cache locality
Linked lists, where random access is O(n)
Data that changes between searches

elements.meaning: A variant that guesses the position from the value's distance between the bounds, reaching O(log log n) on uniformly distributed data.
elements.example: Looking up a name in a phone book by opening near where you expect it.

points: Sorted access is the price of admission
A hash map beats it for pure point lookups
Range queries are where it still wins
